items.name: monomorphism and epimorphism
items.statement_summary: In any category C, an arrow f:A→B is a monomorphism (mono) if it is left-cancellable — for all g,h:C→A, fg=fh implies g=h — and an epimorphism (epi) if it is right-cancellable — for all i,j:B→D, if=jf implies i=j. Notation: f:A↣B for mono, f:A↠B for epi.

items.name: monic iff injective (in Sets)
items.statement_summary: A function f:A→B in Sets is a monomorphism if and only if it is injective. (Proof probes elements with maps from a one-element set.)

items.name: monos in categories of structured sets
items.statement_summary: In categories of 'structured sets' (monoids, groups, rings, vector spaces, posets), the monomorphisms are exactly the homomorphisms whose underlying function is injective: h:M→N is monic iff |h| is monic (injective). Proven for Mon using the free monoid M(*) on one generator to probe elements; the analogue in other algebraic categories follows from existence of a suitable free object.

items.name: every arrow in a poset is mono and epi
items.statement_summary: In a poset P regarded as a category, every arrow p≤q is both monic and epic (cancellation is automatic since each hom-set has at most one arrow).

items.name: N↣Z is a non-surjective epi in Mon
items.statement_summary: In Mon, the inclusion N↪Z of the additive monoid of naturals into the additive monoid of integers is a monomorphism that is also an epimorphism despite not being surjective: any two monoid homomorphisms f,g:(Z,+,0)→(M,*,u) that agree on N are equal (shown via forcing f(-1)=g(-1)). Demonstrates that epis need not be surjective outside Sets.

items.name: every iso is mono and epi
items.statement_summary: Every isomorphism is both monic and epic. Proof: an iso m with inverse e cancels on the left (mx=my implies x=emx=emy=y) and dually e cancels on the right.

items.name: Sets is balanced (mono+epi implies iso)
items.statement_summary: In Sets the converse of Proposition 2.6 holds: every arrow that is both monic and epic is an isomorphism (Sets is 'balanced'). This fails in general categories — the mono-epi N↣Z in Mon is not an iso.

items.name: initial and terminal object
items.statement_summary: In any category C, an object 0 is initial if for every object C there is a unique morphism 0→C; an object 1 is terminal if for every object C there is a unique morphism C→1. A terminal object of C is exactly an initial object of C^op.

items.name: initial/terminal objects unique up to isomorphism
items.statement_summary: Initial objects (and terminal objects) are unique up to a unique isomorphism: if C and C' are both initial (resp. both terminal), there is a unique iso C→C'.

items.name: initial/terminal objects across categories
items.statement_summary: Enumerates initial/terminal objects: (1) in Sets ∅ is initial and any singleton terminal (one initial, many terminals); (2) in Cat the empty category 0 is initial and the one-object one-arrow category 1 terminal; (3) in Groups/Vect/Mon the one-element (zero) object is both initial and terminal, while in Rings Z is initial and the zero ring (0=1) terminal; (4) in Bool the two-element algebra 2 is initial and the one-element algebra terminal; (5) in a poset initial = least element, terminal = greatest element, and a category (e.g. (Z,≤)) may have neither; (6) for any category C and object X, the identity 1_X is terminal in the slice C/X and initial in the coslice X/C.

items.name: Boolean algebra (and the category Bool)
items.statement_summary: A Boolean algebra is a poset B with distinguished elements 0,1, binary operations ∨ (join) and ∧ (meet), and a unary ¬ (complement) satisfying: 0≤a; a≤1; (a≤c and b≤c) iff a∨b≤c; (c≤a and c≤b) iff c≤a∧b; a≤¬b iff a∧b=0; ¬¬a=a. Example: the powerset P(X) ordered by inclusion (0=∅, 1=X, join/meet = union/intersection, ¬A = X−A); the two-element algebra 2={0,1} is 'truth values'. The category Bool has Boolean algebras as objects and Boolean homomorphisms h:B→B' (preserving 0,1,∨,∧) as arrows. Defined in running prose within Example 2.9(4).

items.name: filter in a Boolean algebra
items.statement_summary: A filter in a Boolean algebra B is a non-empty subset F⊆B that is closed upward and under meets: a∈F and a≤b imply b∈F; a∈F and b∈F imply a∧b∈F. Defined in running prose.

items.name: ultrafilter (maximal filter)
items.statement_summary: A filter F is maximal — an ultrafilter — if the only filter F' with F⊂F' strictly larger is all of B; equivalently, F is an ultrafilter iff for every b∈B exactly one of b∈F, ¬b∈F holds (stated as an exercise). Defined in running prose.

items.name: Boolean homs B→2 correspond to ultrafilters
items.statement_summary: For a Boolean algebra B, Boolean homomorphisms p:B→2 (into the initial algebra) correspond bijectively to ultrafilters U⊆B via U_p = p^{-1}(1) and, conversely, p_U(b)=1 iff b∈U; the two operations are mutually inverse. (Underlies truth-value/truth-table valuations.) Developed in running prose.

items.name: global element / point / constant
items.statement_summary: In a category with terminal object 1, an arrow 1→A is a global element (also 'point' or 'constant') of A. In Sets there is an iso X ≅ Hom(1,X) between elements and points (and similarly for posets/spaces). A category 'has enough points' when f,g:A→B are equal iff fa=ga for every point a:1→A — true in Sets, Pos, Top, but false in Mon, where each object has a single point. Defined in running prose.

items.name: having enough points vs. generalized elements
items.statement_summary: (1) In Pos, f,g:X→Y are equal iff fx=gx for all points x:1→X (posets have enough points). (2) In Mon, homs h,j:M→N always agree on the unique point x:1→M, so monoids lack enough points. (3) In any category C, f,g:C→C' are equal iff fx=gx for all generalized elements x:D→C (every object has enough generalized elements). (4) It often suffices to use generalized elements of a fixed 'test' shape T→A.

items.name: generalized element / variable element
items.statement_summary: A generalized (variable) element of an object A is an arbitrary arrow x:X→A with any domain X; global elements are the case X=1. Logicians read 1→A as constants/closed terms and X→A as arbitrary terms. Motivated by the fact that objects are generally not determined by their global points. Defined in running prose.

items.name: generalized elements reveal structure; Hom(2,−) invariant
items.statement_summary: The posets A={a≤b≤c} (a 3-chain) and X={x≤y, x≤z} admit an order-preserving bijection f:X→A (f(x)=a, f(y)=b, f(z)=c) that is monic and epic in Pos but not an isomorphism. Although X and A have equally many global elements (3 each), the counts of 2-elements (arrows 2→−, i.e. |Hom(2,−)|) differ — X has 5, A has 6 — and since |Hom(2,P)| is an isomorphism invariant (an iso P≅Q induces a bijection Hom(2,P)≅Hom(2,Q) by post-composition, f_*(h)=fh), X and A are not isomorphic. Illustrates defining invariants via generalized elements.

items.name: figures of shape T; |M| ≅ Hom_Mon(M(*),M)
items.statement_summary: Generalized elements t:T→A 'based at' a test object T are geometric 'figures of shape T in A' (like an arrow 2→P being an inequality p≤p' in a poset P). In Mon, arrows from the terminal monoid 1 are uninformative, but arrows from the free monoid M(*) on one generator suffice to separate homomorphisms; indeed the underlying set |M| ≅ Hom_Mon(M(*),M). Sits at the top of PDF p49, still within §2.3 (above the §2.4 header).

items.name: an arrow with a left inverse is monic (its retraction epic)
items.statement_summary: If an arrow f:A→B has a left inverse g:B→A (gf=1_A), then f is monic and g is epic (stated as an easy exercise). Generalizes 'every iso is mono and epi'; motivates Definition 2.13. Stated in running prose leading into §2.4.

items.name: split mono/epi, section, retraction, retract
items.statement_summary: A split mono (resp. split epi) is an arrow with a left (resp. right) inverse. If e:X→A and s:A→X satisfy es=1_A, then s is a section (or splitting) of e and e is a retraction of s; the object A is a retract of X.

items.name: functors preserve split monos and split epis
items.statement_summary: Since functors preserve identities (and composition), they preserve split monos and split epis. Contrast the forgetful functor Mon→Set, which fails to preserve the (non-split) epi N→Z.

items.name: splittings in Sets; every epi splits = axiom of choice
items.statement_summary: In Sets every mono splits except those of the form ∅↣A. 'Every epi splits' is the categorical axiom of choice: for an epi e:E↠X, a splitting s:X→E (es=1_X) is exactly a choice function for the family of nonempty fibers E_x=e^{-1}{x}; conversely any family of nonempty sets yields such an epi whose splittings are its choice functions.

items.name: projective object
items.statement_summary: An object P is projective if for every epi e:E↠X and every arrow f:P→X there exists a (not necessarily unique) arrow f̄:P→E with e∘f̄=f (one says f 'lifts across' e). Under the axiom of choice all sets are projective; free objects in many (not all) algebraic categories are projective; any retract of a projective object is projective. Defined in running prose (still §2.4, above the §2.5 header).

items.name: product diagram (universal mapping property)
items.statement_summary: In any category C, a product diagram for objects A and B is an object P with projections A ←p1— P —p2→ B satisfying the UMP: for every diagram A ←x1— X —x2→ B there is a unique u:X→P with p1u=x1 and p2u=x2. Obtained from the set-theoretic cartesian product A×B={(a,b)} with coordinate projections π1,π2 by replacing elements with generalized elements.

items.name: two parts of the product UMP (existence and uniqueness)
items.statement_summary: Spells out the product UMP as two parts: Existence, there is some mediating u : X -> P with x1 = p1 o u and x2 = p2 o u; and Uniqueness, any v : X -> P with p1 o v = x1 and p2 o v = x2 must equal u.

items.name: products are unique up to isomorphism
items.statement_summary: Any two product diagrams (P,p1,p2) and (Q,q1,q2) for the same pair A,B are canonically isomorphic: the induced mediating maps i : P -> Q and j : Q -> P (with q_k o i = p_k and p_k o j = q_k) satisfy j o i = 1_P and i o j = 1_Q by the uniqueness clause, so i is an iso commuting with the projections. Proof given.

items.name: worked example: cartesian product as the product in Sets
items.statement_summary: The cartesian product A x B with its two projections is a product in Sets; different set-theoretic encodings of ordered pairs (e.g. Kuratowski <a,b> = {{a},{a,b}} versus <a,b>' = <a,<a,b>>) each give a product, and any two are isomorphic.

items.name: worked example: componentwise product of monoids/groups
items.statement_summary: For monoids or groups G,H the categorical product G x H is the cartesian product of underlying sets equipped with componentwise operation <g,h> . <g',h'> = <g.g', h.h'>, unit <u_G,u_H>, and (for groups) inverse <a,b>^-1 = <a^-1,b^-1>; the two projections are homomorphisms, giving the product in Grp/Mon.

items.name: worked example: product category as the product in Cat
items.statement_summary: For (small) categories C and D, the previously defined product category C x D of pairs of objects and arrows, together with its two projection functors, is the product in Cat; products of posets and of monoids arise as special cases.

items.name: worked example: product in a poset is the greatest lower bound (meet)
items.statement_summary: In a poset P viewed as a category, the product p x q of two elements is their greatest lower bound (meet) p /\ q: it satisfies p x q <= p and p x q <= q, and whenever x <= p and x <= q then x <= p x q.

items.name: worked example: product of topological spaces in Top
items.statement_summary: The usual product space X x Y (product topology generated by basic opens U x V, U in O(X), V in O(Y)) with its projections p1,p2 is the product in Top: projections are continuous (p1^-1 U = U x 1_Y), and for continuous f1 : Z -> X, f2 : Z -> Y the pairing <f1,f2> is continuous, shown via f^-1(U x V) = (f1)^-1(U) intersect (f2)^-1(V).

items.name: category of types C(lambda) of the simply-typed lambda-calculus (with binary products)
items.statement_summary: Builds the category of types C(lambda): objects are types (base types closed under x and ->), arrows A -> B are closed lambda-terms c : A -> B identified up to beta-eta-equivalence (generated by fst<a,b>=a, snd<a,b>=b, <fst c, snd c>=c, (lambda x.b)a = b[a/x], lambda x.cx = c, plus bound renaming), identity 1_A = lambda x.x, composition c o b = lambda x.c(bx); unit and associativity laws are verified. Shows C(lambda) has binary products A x B with projections p1 = lambda z.fst(z), p2 = lambda z.snd(z) and pairing (a,b) = lambda x.<ax,bx> satisfying the product UMP.

items.name: product of morphisms and the product functor x : C x C -> C
items.statement_summary: In a category with a chosen product for each pair, defines the product of two morphisms f x f' = <f o p1, f' o p2> : A x A' -> B x B' (making both projection squares commute) and observes that choosing products for all pairs assembles these into a bifunctor x : C x C -> C.

items.name: has binary products
items.statement_summary: A category is said to have binary products if it has a product diagram for every pair of objects.

items.name: finite (ternary / n-ary) products from binary products; associativity up to iso
items.statement_summary: Defines ternary products A1 x A2 x A3 and general n-ary products by the analogous UMP (n projections p_i, and for any X with arrows x_i a unique u with p_i o u = x_i); shows a category with binary products has all finite products with two or more factors, e.g. A x B x C := (A x B) x C, and that the binary product is associative up to isomorphism (A x B) x C ~= A x (B x C).

items.name: terminal object as nullary product; unary product
items.statement_summary: Observes that a terminal object 1 is the nullary (empty) product, the unique arrow ! : X -> 1 serving as the mediating map with no projections to match, and that any object A is its own unary product.

items.name: product of an I-indexed family of objects
items.statement_summary: Introduces the product of a family (C_i)_{i in I} indexed by an arbitrary set I via an I-ary UMP generalizing the nullary/unary/binary/n-ary cases; the precise formulation of this UMP is left to Exercise 7.

items.name: has all finite products / has all (small) products
items.statement_summary: A category C has all finite products if it has a terminal object and all binary products (hence products of any finite cardinality); C has all (small) products if every set of objects in C has a product.

items.name: Hom-set and the induced post-composition map g_*
items.statement_summary: In a locally small category, Hom(A,B) denotes the set of arrows A -> B (a Hom-set); each arrow g : B -> B' induces the post-composition function Hom(A,g) = g_* : Hom(A,B) -> Hom(A,B') sending f to g o f.

items.name: covariant representable functor Hom(A,-) : C -> Sets
items.statement_summary: Shows Hom(A,-) : C -> Sets is a functor: on objects B |-> Hom(A,B), on arrows g |-> g_* = g o -; verifies functoriality Hom(A, 1_X) = 1_{Hom(A,X)} and Hom(A, g o f) = Hom(A,g) o Hom(A,f).

items.name: Hom-set characterization of products
items.statement_summary: A diagram A <-p1- P -p2-> B is a product for A and B iff for every object X the canonical comparison function theta_X = (Hom(X,p1), Hom(X,p2)) : Hom(X,P) -> Hom(X,A) x Hom(X,B), sending x to (p1 o x, p2 o x) (equation 2.1), is a bijection/isomorphism. Proof: the UMP says exactly that each (x1,x2) has a unique preimage, i.e. theta_X is bijective.

items.name: functor preserving binary products
items.statement_summary: A functor F : C -> D between categories with binary products preserves binary products if it sends every product diagram A <- A x B -> B in C to a product diagram FA <- F(A x B) -> FB in D; equivalently iff the canonical comparison arrow <Fp1, Fp2> : F(A x B) -> FA x FB is an iso (F(A x B) ~= FA x FB canonically). Example: the forgetful U : Mon -> Sets preserves binary products.

items.name: covariant representable functors preserve products
items.statement_summary: For any object X in a category C with products, the covariant representable functor Hom_C(X,-) : C -> Sets preserves products, giving the canonical iso Hom(X, A x B) ~= Hom(X,A) x Hom(X,B); follows from Proposition 2.20.

items.name: surjection equals epimorphism in Sets
items.statement_summary: Show that a function between sets is surjective iff it is an epimorphism in Sets.

items.name: mono/epi/iso propagation across a commutative triangle
items.statement_summary: For a commutative triangle h = g o f (f : A -> B, g : B -> C, h : A -> C) in any category, show: (a) if f and g are both isos (resp. both monos, resp. both epis) then so is h; (b) if h is monic then f is monic; (c) if h is epic then g is epic; (d) by an example, if h is monic then g need not be.

items.name: projective objects: sets, posets, retracts
items.statement_summary: Using the axiom of choice, show every set is projective; show that the epis among posets are the surjections (on objects) and that the one-element poset 1 is projective; and show that in any category a retract of a projective object is projective.

items.name: A-monoids: initial object equals free monoid
items.statement_summary: For a set A, define an A-monoid to be a monoid M with a function m : A -> U(M), and a morphism of A-monoids h : (M,m) -> (N,n) to be a monoid homomorphism h : M -> N with U(h) o m = n, forming a category A-Mon. Show that an initial object of A-Mon is the same thing as a free monoid M(A) on A (by comparing their UMPs).

items.name: boolean homomorphisms to 2 correspond to ultrafilters
items.statement_summary: Show that for any boolean algebra B, boolean homomorphisms h : B -> 2 correspond exactly to ultrafilters in B.

items.name: associativity of binary products up to iso
items.statement_summary: Show that in any category with binary products, A x (B x C) ~= (A x B) x C.

items.name: I-indexed products; X^I as a product in Sets
items.statement_summary: (a) For any index set I, define the product prod_{i in I} X_i of an I-indexed family (X_i)_{i in I} in a category by giving a UMP generalizing that for binary products (the case I = 2). (b) Show that in Sets the set X^I of all functions f : I -> X satisfies this UMP with respect to the constant family X_i = X for all i in I, so X^I ~= prod_{i in I} X.
